newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan court orders Bhutto's husband be released.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan court orders Bhutto's husband be released.

text.p: A Pakistan court on Wednesday ordered the release of Asif Ali Zardari, husband of ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, after it ruled his detention void, Pakistan People's Party (PPP) leaders said.
A spokesman for Bhutto's party said a two-judge Division Bench of the Sindh High Court in Karachi had declared Zardari's detention on public order charges void and ordered his release.
Farooq Naik, an advocate for Zardari, said the investment minister in Bhutto's ousted government was expected to be released on Thursday after some procedures were completed.
"Zardari is likely to be released tomorrow if he is not detained in any other case," Naik added.
Prison officials said they were still waiting for an order to set Zardari free.
"We have not yet received release papers (for) Zardari," one official told Reuters.
Witnesses outside the prison said more than two dozen armed police were guarding the entrance of the jail where dozens of PPP supporters carrying garlands and gifts had gathered to welcome Zardari.
A spokesman for Bhutto welcomed the court decision but said it was not clear if the government would let Zardari go or detain him on some other "trumped up charge".
He said Bhutto would go to Karachi on Thursday from Lahore where she was meeting party leaders and workers to prepare for elections set for February 3.
The court passed the order on a constitutional petition filed by Zardari's sister, Faryal Talpur, a court official said.
President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
Soon afterwards her husband was detained in the city of Lahore under the catch-all Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance.
He was transferred to a resthouse near Islamabad before being sent to Karachi on November 27.
Bhutto and Zardari have been at the centre of corruption allegations associated with the former government. Both deny any wrongdoing.
